value.overview: The American Oystercatcher is a large coastal shorebird named for its ability to open oysters and other shellfish. It has striking black-and-white plumage, a long bright orange-red bill, yellow eyes, and a red eye ring. The species occupies sandy and rocky shores, tidal flats, shell beaches, salt marshes, and offshore islands. In Costa Rica it is uncommon and localized, occurring mainly along suitable Pacific coastal habitats and nearby islands.
value.classification: The American Oystercatcher belongs to the order Charadriiformes and the oystercatcher family, Haematopodidae. Its scientific name is Haematopus palliatus.
value.identification: This robust shorebird has a black head, neck, and upper breast, dark brown to black upperparts, and a white belly. The long, thick bill is orange-red, often with a darker tip. Adults show bright yellow eyes surrounded by a narrow red orbital ring. In flight, the white underparts contrast with dark wings and a broad white wing stripe. Its large size, vivid bill, and pied pattern distinguish it from other Costa Rican shorebirds.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs along coastlines from North and Central America through much of South America. In Costa Rica, it is a rare or uncommon coastal bird, recorded mainly on remote Pacific beaches, rocky shores, tidal flats, estuaries, and small offshore islands. Breeding has been reported on Bolaños Island in the Gulf of Papagayo, while other observations may involve resident birds or occasional movements along the Pacific coast. It is not a species of inland habitats.
value.migrationStatus: The American Oystercatcher is partly migratory across its broad range. Many northern birds move south after breeding, while populations in tropical Central America are resident or locally dispersive. In Costa Rica it occurs in small numbers, especially along the Pacific coast and nearby islands; individuals from farther north may also reach the country, as shown by a bird banded in Florida and recorded in Guanacaste.
value.breeding: Pairs usually nest on open, sparsely vegetated sand, shell, gravel, or rocky ground above the highest tides. The nest is a shallow scrape, often placed on beaches, dunes, salt-marsh edges, sandbars, or islands. Both adults defend the territory and incubate the eggs. Chicks leave the nest soon after hatching but depend on the adults for protection and guidance. In Costa Rica, breeding is documented at least locally on Bolaños Island, although the national breeding population is small.
value.dietFeeding: The main foods are marine mollusks, including oysters, clams, mussels, limpets, and other bivalves and gastropods. It also takes crabs, worms, other marine invertebrates, and occasionally small fish or insects. The strong, laterally compressed bill is used in different ways: birds may hammer shells open, pry them apart, or stab soft-bodied prey. Feeding normally takes place on exposed intertidal flats, shell beds, rocky shores, and oyster reefs.
value.behavior: American Oystercatchers are usually seen alone, in pairs, or in small family groups. They walk deliberately along the shoreline while probing or inspecting exposed shellfish. Pairs are strongly territorial during breeding and give loud, ringing calls when alarmed. Adults may confront predators or intruders near nests and chicks. Outside the breeding season, birds often roost on undisturbed beaches, sandbars, mudflats, or islands during high tide.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not uniformly documented and varies among regions. Northern populations have experienced local declines, while some protected or managed populations are stable or increasing. The small Costa Rican population is considered uncommon, but a precise national trend is not available.
